analysis.one_liner: Freezes HHS's new organ-allocation rule for one year, keeping the current local-first transplant system in place.
analysis.headline: Backed by 29 senators from both parties, the bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1998 the Department of Health and Human Services issued a final rule that would change how scarce donor organs are handed out, shifting away from a local-first system toward allocating organs to the sickest patients over wider areas. This bill would have voided that rule for one year, barred the Secretary of Health and Human Services from changing the existing organ-allocation regulations during that time, and required the Secretary to study how the changes would affect poor patients, access, survival rates, and waiting times before making them.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have benefited the existing transplant system's incumbents: organ procurement organizations and transplant centers that operate under the current local-first allocation rules would keep their roles and patient flows for at least another year. The bill's own findings also argue the delay protects patients, claiming the HHS rule would make transplants economically prohibitive for many, including the roughly 22 percent of transplant recipients on Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Transplant centers and organ procurement groups

how_it_helps.text: The bill would void the HHS final rule (the new part 121 of federal regulations) and bar the Secretary from modifying organ-allocation regulations for one year, keeping the existing system in place while alternatives were developed.

During the moratorium, the Secretary would have to consult with the medical community and organ donation organizations, including those serving low-income patients, to develop new guidelines for operating the transplant network.

Before any changes take effect, the Secretary would have to study the impact on indigent care, economic and geographic access, transplant outcomes and survival rates, and waiting-list times by organ, then open the plan to at least 90 days of public comment.

analysis.who_pays: The people who bear the cost of a passed bill would be patients on the waiting list, especially those in areas with few donated organs. Under the existing system the bill preserves, where a patient lives largely determines whether they get an organ; the bill's own findings note that about 60,000 Americans were waiting and 11 people on the list died each day while the allocation debate continued.

drawbacks.text: A one-year delay prolongs a system in which geographic location, rather than medical urgency, largely decides who receives an organ. The bill's own findings acknowledge the stakes: every 16 minutes a name is added to the waiting list and 11 people on it die each day.

The bill voids a rule that had already gone through the federal rulemaking process, substituting a further study-and-comment period for the changes the Secretary had concluded were needed, which pushes any reform out by at least a year.

The bill's sponsors' strongest good-faith concern is that eliminating geographic criteria could make transplants economically prohibitive for some patients, particularly the roughly 22 percent of recipients covered by Medicaid, by shifting transplants to fewer, larger centers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A one-year pause with mandated study and public comment sounds reasonable, and the concerns about cost and access for poor and rural patients deserve study. But the pause protects the status quo, in which a patient's chance of survival depends heavily on where they live, and the bill's own findings describe the daily death toll while allocation rules remain unchanged. The delay's main practical effect is to give incumbent transplant centers and organ procurement organizations another year under the old system.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was filed, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Torricelli introduced the bill on June 22, 1998, joined by 14 original cosponsors including senators from both parties such as Gorton, Feingold, Mack, Thurmond, Landrieu, and Hollings.
Twenty-nine senators cosponsored the bill in total: 18 Republicans and 11 Democrats.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day it was introduced; the action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the HHS allocation rule faced no one-year bar from this bill, and patients whose access depended on changing the local-first system were spared the delay the bill would have imposed. Transplant centers and organ procurement organizations did not get the moratorium they sought through this vehicle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients waiting for the HHS rule

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to delay the HHS organ-allocation rule and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 18 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to delay the rule.

for.name: 11 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill to delay the rule.

for.name: Organ procurement organizations and the United Network for Organ Sharing
for.role: Operators of the existing organ-donation and transplant network
for.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the HHS allocation rule and supported delaying it, arguing the new rules would disrupt local donation systems.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Jim Jeffords, R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the referred bill; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: HHS Secretary Donna Shalala
against.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
against.what_they_did: Issued the final rule the bill sought to void, which would have shifted organ allocation toward medical urgency over broader geographic areas.

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines: 18 of the Senate's 55 Republicans and 11 of its 45 Democrats cosponsored the bill introduced by a Democrat, yet it never received a committee vote.

industries.note: The HHS rule would have shifted allocation away from local-first distribution, weakening OPOs' gatekeeping over which patients get organs. The bill's one-year moratorium would have preserved their control of the system while roughly 60,000 people waited, many in organ-poor regions.

High-volume centers in areas with plentiful donations benefit from the local-first status quo the bill preserves; centers in organ-poor areas would gain patients under the HHS rule. The bill's sponsors argue delaying the rule protects access for Medicaid-covered recipients, but the delay also keeps survival chances tied to geography.

industries.industry: United Network for Organ Sharing (network operator)
industries.note: The private nonprofit that runs the transplant network would have kept operating under existing rules during the moratorium, avoiding federal override of its allocation policies.
